**Who meets whom, and why does it matter?** So far, everyone in the town mixes equally. In reality, children have more contacts than adults, mostly with other children; people travel between towns; and some infections pass only between people who know each other, such as sexual partners. This tutorial goes from equal mixing, to a contact matrix between age groups, to movement between places, to contacts between particular people.

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- split a model into age groups, give a value for each, and read results by group;
- give the contacts between groups as a contact matrix, and say what β means then;
- give a model several places, linked by movement, and see how chance affects the spread;
- use networks (random and sexual) and mixing pools, and choose between them.

## Age groups, each with its own immunity

This starts from the SEIR measles model of [T3 – Building a disease](t3_disease.qmd), in a town of 100,000 people (R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15). `stratify()` splits each state into groups: here by age, into 0–14, 15–64, and 65 and over, each given by its lower edge with its share of the population (30%, 60%, and 10%).

Age groups matter when something differs between them, such as immunity. Suppose 92% of adults under 65 and 98% of older adults are immune, but only 80% of children, since vaccine coverage has slipped. [`ss.by()`](../api/internals.parameters.qmd) gives a value for each age group, and `init` the share of each group that starts in a state; `init_n` starts 10 people infectious, as if brought in by travelers:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                           # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
equal = ss.Sim(measles, label='Everyone mixes equally', **settings)
equal.run()
equal.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

About 90% of the town is immune, so each case at the start infects about 1.7 others (printed as `R` at the start): a modest outbreak, spread over the age groups in proportion to the susceptible people in each.

## Contacts between age groups

A **contact matrix** gives the daily contacts between age groups: row *i*, column *j* is the number of contacts one person in group *i* has with people in group *j*, as measured by contact surveys such as POLYMOD. The numbers below are illustrative, but shaped like real surveys: children mix most, mostly with each other.

| Contacts a day, of a person aged... | ...with people 0–14 | ...with people 15–64 | ...with people 65+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–14 | 10 | 6 | 1 |
| 15–64 | 3 | 8 | 1 |
| 65+ | 3 | 6 | 3 |

[`ss.contacts()`](../api/networks.qmd) takes the matrix, with the lower edge of each age group (`ages=`), and is given to the sim as `networks=`. With contacts, β is the daily rate of infection per contact with an infectious person. People here average about 13.5 contacts a day, so β = 1.9 under equal mixing becomes about 0.14 per contact: a β fitted under one assumption about mixing needs refitting under another.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # At a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=contacts, label='Contact matrix', **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
beta <- par(0.14, bounds = c(0.05, 0.5)) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = Transition(S, E, rate = beta * I), # At a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)),
  recovery    = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),
  init   = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))),
  init_n = list(I = 10)
)
measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1))

age_contacts <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(10, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3))) # Contacts a day, between age groups
sim <- Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", label = "Contact matrix")
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$infection$by("age")$plot()
```

## Explicit

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='E'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
beta_explicit = ss.par(ss.perday(0.14), bounds=[ss.perday(0.05), ss.perday(0.5)], name='beta') # Per contact with an infectious person

measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=E, rate=beta_explicit*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10)), name='progression'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery'),
    ],
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The rest start in S
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name   = 'measles',
)
measles_explicit.stratify(age=ss.levels({0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, kind='age')) # Age groups, which people would age through

contacts_explicit = ss.contacts(matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], ages=[0, 15, 65], name='contacts')
sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = contacts_explicit,
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = '2025-01-01',
    stop      = '2026-01-01',
    dt        = ss.days(1),
    unit      = 'day',
    solver    = 'ode',
    aging     = False, # Nobody is born or dies, so nobody ages
    label     = 'Contact matrix',
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```
:::

The reproduction number at the start is now about 2.5 rather than 1.7, since the susceptible people are children, who have the most contacts:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel([equal, sim])
msim.plot('measles.infection')
```

With the contact matrix, the outbreak peaks sooner and higher, and infects more people, the extra ones all children: assuming equal mixing underestimates an outbreak where the gaps in immunity are in the group that mixes most.

### Results by age group

A stratified model keeps every result for each group, and totals as before. [`by('age')`](../api/results.qmd) splits a result into a series per age group, and `select()` picks one group by its ages (`'0-14'`, `'15-64'`, `'65+'`):

```{python}
res = sim.results.measles
children = res.I.select(age='0-14')
print('Peak number of children infectious:', round(children.max()))
print('Infections in people 65 and over:', round(res.infection.select(age='65+').sum()))
```

`summarize()` gives each group's total over the run. Dividing by each group's size gives the share infected (the attack rate), the risk:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
infections = res.infection.by('age').summarize()
print(infections.round())
print('Share of each group infected:')
print((infections / [30_000, 60_000, 10_000]).round(3))
```

## R

```r
res <- sim$results$measles
infections <- res$infection$by("age")$summarize()
print(round(infections))
cat("Share of each group infected:\n")
print(round(infections / c(30000, 60000, 10000), 3))
```

## Explicit

```{python}
sizes = {'0-14': 30_000, '15-64': 60_000, '65+': 10_000}
for age, size in sizes.items():
    total = res.infection.select(age=age).sum()
    print(age, ' infections:', round(total), ' share infected:', round(total/size, 3))
```
:::

Children have nearly two thirds of the infections, though under a third of the town. For more on stratification, see [T7 – Stratification and co-transmission](t7_strata.qmd) and [Stratification](../user_guide/building_stratification.qmd).

## Several towns

People travel between towns, and carry measles with them. A **metapopulation** model has several populations coupled by movement. A function makes the disease as above, with the number infectious at the start given; its latent and infectious states are marked as infected, so that the results `infected` and `prevalence` count them:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, R = ss.states('S R')
E, I = ss.states('E I', infected=True) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

def make_measles(init_n=10):
    """ The measles model, by age, with the number infectious at the start given """
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
        init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
        init_n = dict(I=init_n),
        name   = 'measles',
    )
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
    return measles
```

## R

```r
states("S R")
states("E I", infected = TRUE) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
infection   <- Transition(S, E, rate = beta * I)
progression <- Transition(E, I, dur = days(10))
recovery    <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))

make_measles <- function(init_n = 10) {
  measles <- Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = list(I = init_n),
    name   = "measles"
  )
  measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
  measles
}
```
:::

The town, Riverton, has three smaller neighbors. A **geography** ([`ss.geo.geography()`](../api/geo.qmd)) gives the places' names, populations, and positions (here in kilometers):

```{python}
towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names       = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeview', 'Fairfield'],
    populations = [100_000, 40_000, 20_000, 10_000],
    x           = [0, 20, 35, 60], # Kilometers east of Riverton
    y           = [0, 10, -15, 5], # Kilometers north of Riverton
)
towns.plot()
```

Places are a stratification, like age groups: `stratify(patch=...)` splits each state by town (a "patch" is a place in a metapopulation model), and the contact matrix applies within each town. `ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0])` starts the outbreak in Riverton only.

Movement is rarely known in detail. A **gravity model** is the usual first guess: movement grows with the destination's population and falls with the square of the distance. Its amount is the share of time people spend in other towns, `away`, here 1%. Written out, it is a matrix of the share of time each town's people spend in each other town:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
away = ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]) # People spend 1% of their time in other towns
settings = dict(networks=contacts, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
measles = make_measles(init_n=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0]))
measles.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=away)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```

## R

```r
towns <- ss$geo$geography(
  names       = c("Riverton", "Hillside", "Lakeview", "Fairfield"),
  populations = c(100000, 40000, 20000, 10000),
  x           = c(0, 20, 35, 60), # Kilometers east of Riverton
  y           = c(0, 10, -15, 5)  # Kilometers north of Riverton
)
away <- par(0.01, bounds = c(0.001, 0.1)) # People spend 1% of their time in other towns
measles <- make_measles(init_n = ss$by(patch = c(10, 0, 0, 0)))
measles$stratify(patch = ss$levels(towns, mobility = ss$geo$gravity(away = away)))

sim <- Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01")
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$I$by("patch")$plot()
```

## Explicit

```{python}
import numpy as np

pop, dist = towns.populations, towns.distances
with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
    pull = pop[None, :]/dist**2 # Gravity: the destination's population over the squared distance
np.fill_diagonal(pull, 0)       # Staying at home isn't movement
share = 0.01*pull/pull.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) # 1% of each town's time away, split by pull

moving = make_measles(init_n=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0]))
moving.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.Mobility(share, kind='commute')))

by_hand = ss.Sim(moving, **settings)
by_hand.run()
by_hand.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```
:::

This is commuting: people keep their home town, but spend a share of their time in the others. (Migration, in which people move home, is `kind='migrate'`.) When movement is known, from a survey or mobile phone data, give it as a matrix, as in the explicit tab. The outbreak peaks first in Riverton, then in each other town in turn, last in Fairfield, the smallest and farthest. `select(patch='Fairfield')` picks one place's result, as it does an age group's.

`map()` draws a result on a map of the places; prevalence suits it better than counts, since the towns differ in size. `animate=True` makes an animation (press play); [Places](../user_guide/populations_places.qmd#maps) has the other options, and [Mixing](../user_guide/populations_mixing.qmd) the radiation model and other ways to couple places:

```{python}
sim.results.measles.prevalence.map(animate=True)
```

### Chance

In this ODE model, measles always reaches Fairfield: a fraction of an infectious person can travel there on day one. In reality, a whole infectious person must go, and the chains of infection they start can die out by chance. To see this, run the model as a stochastic model (`solver='binomial'`; [T5](t5_interventions.qmd#many-runs) says more), with a tenth as much movement (`pars=dict(away=0.001)`), many times:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(away=0.001), solver='binomial', **settings)
msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=30)
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Fairfield').plot(lines=True)
```

```{python}
fairfield = msim.results.measles.infection.select(patch='Fairfield').summarize() # The infections in Fairfield in each run
print('Runs with an outbreak in Fairfield:', sum(fairfield > 100), 'of', len(fairfield))
```

In some runs, measles never takes off in Fairfield, and in the others it comes at very different times. For a small, weakly linked place, whether an outbreak arrives at all is a matter of chance. The same model also runs as agents (`n_agents=170_000`), each with a home town and an age group, who age, are born, and die ([T6](t6_data.qmd#births-and-deaths)).

## Contacts per person

Random mixing within age groups and towns suits measles. A sexually transmitted infection instead spreads between partners who stay together for months, and HIV passes from mother to child. Then who is linked with whom, and for how long, matters: that is what a **network** describes. Starsim has two ways to transmit disease between people, which can be used together:

- **Contact networks:** disease transmits along links (edges) between agents, which can change each step.
- **Mixing pools:** well-mixed transmission from one group to another, as with a contact matrix, without listing who meets whom.

A model with a network runs as agents. To see when a network matters, take the measles model of [T1](t1_intro.qmd), with nobody immune, as 10,000 agents. With 3 contacts a day, a rate of 0.63 per contact per day gives the same β of 3 × 0.63 = 1.9 (for a chance per contact instead, give `ss.probperday()`). Those 3 contacts can be arranged in several ways:

- `ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3)`: everyone mixes at random.
- `ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3)`: each person has 3 contacts, new each day.
- `ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False)`: each person has the same 3 contacts for the whole run.

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.63*I       # A rate of infection of 0.63 per contact per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sims = {
    'Well mixed':              ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'New contacts each day':   ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'Same contacts every day': ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

With someone new each day, the epidemic is nearly the same as with random mixing. With the same people every day, it is slower, since contacts are wasted on whoever infected you. Even so, almost everyone is infected, since measles passes along nearly every link. A network matters most when people have few, lasting contacts, each with a chance of infection well below one, as for sexually transmitted infections.

### Looking inside a network

A network's contacts are made when the sim is initialized. Here is one for 30 people, so that it can be plotted:

```{python}
small = ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), n_agents=30, stop=ss.days(10), verbose=0)
small.init()
net = small.networks.randomnet
net.plot()
```

Networks are in `sim.networks`, each under its class name in lower case. Each edge has the UIDs of the two people (`p1` and `p2`), a transmission multiplier (`beta`), and a duration (`dur`). The edges can be converted to a dataframe (`to_df()`) or a NetworkX graph (`to_graph()`):

```{python}
print('Contacts of agent 0:', net.find_contacts([0]))

df = net.to_df()
df.loc[(df.p1 == 0) | (df.p2 == 0)] # The edges involving agent 0
```

## Sexual networks

Take a simplified curable bacterial infection, loosely like gonorrhea: an SIS model, in which people become susceptible again when they recover (after 6 months on average, untreated). `ss.SexualNet()` is a network of partnerships between men and women, each lasting a time (`dur=`), with 80 sex acts a year by default. The chance of infection is given per act with `ss.peract()`, from men to women (`m2f`) and women to men (`f2m`). Here are three networks that differ only in how long partnerships last:

```{python}
S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I  # Chance of infection per act
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)                    # Infected for 6 months on average
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))
sims = {}
for label, dur in {'1 month': ss.months(1), '3 months': ss.months(3), '1 year': ss.years(1)}.items():
    network = ss.SexualNet(dur=dur) # How long partnerships last, on average
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sti, networks=network, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
```

With short partnerships, people have many partners a year, and the infection becomes endemic. When they last a year, a couple infects each other and has no one else to infect; by the time they part, the infection has usually cleared, and it dies out. At any moment, these three networks look alike; only how often partners change differs. `ss.SexualNet()` also sets the number of partners at a time, the age of sexual debut, and who takes part. Transmission from mother to child uses `ss.PrenatalNet()` and its relatives, with `ss.Pregnancy()`. Both are covered in [Mixing](../user_guide/populations_mixing.qmd).

## Mixing pools

A mixing pool suits large groups such as a school or a town, where everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else; a network suits small groups where who meets whom matters, such as households. `source=` and `target=` say who can infect and who can be infected. Here measles spreads through a school, where children aged 5 to 14 have 10 contacts a day with each other, and the community, where everyone has 2 a day. Written out, the condition on `ss.person.age` is a function of the sim that returns the schoolchildren's UIDs:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.19*I       # A chance of infection of 0.19 per contact per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 5, 15]) # Ages 0-4, 5-14, and 15+, for the results
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
school    = ss.MixingPool(name='school', source=(ss.person.age >= 5) & (ss.person.age < 15), target=(ss.person.age >= 5) & (ss.person.age < 15), n_contacts=10)
community = ss.MixingPool(name='community', n_contacts=2)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=[school, community], n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

## R

```r
# The measles model above
states("S I R")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = 0.19 * I) # A chance of infection of 0.19 per contact per day
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))
measles <- Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev = 0.001)
measles$stratify(age = c(0, 5, 15)) # Ages 0-4, 5-14, and 15+, for the results

school_age <- (ss$person$age >= 5) & (ss$person$age < 15)
school    <- ss$MixingPool(name = "school", source = school_age, target = school_age, n_contacts = 10)
community <- ss$MixingPool(name = "community", n_contacts = 2)
sim <- Sim(measles, networks = list(school, community), n_agents = 10000, stop = days(100))
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$infection$by("age")$plot()
```

## Explicit

```{python}
def school_age(sim):
    """ The UIDs of the children aged 5 to 14 """
    age = sim.people.age
    return age.auids[(age.values >= 5) & (age.values < 15)]

school    = ss.MixingPool(name='school', source=school_age, target=school_age, n_contacts=10)
community = ss.MixingPool(name='community', n_contacts=2)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=[school, community], n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```
:::

The epidemic starts in school-age children and spreads to the rest of the community. A set of mixing pools by age is a contact matrix: `ss.contacts()` makes one pool for each pair of age groups.

### Choosing how people mix

| How people meet | Use | Runs as |
|---|---|---|
| Many brief contacts, at random | No network (homogeneous mixing), or `ss.MixingPool()` | Compartments or agents |
| At random, but more within some groups (e.g. by age) | `ss.contacts()` with a stratified disease | Compartments or agents |
| The same few people, again and again (households, partners) | A network: `ss.RandomNet(dynamic=False)`, `ss.SexualNet()`, or the library's household networks | Agents |
| From mother to child | `ss.PrenatalNet()`, with `ss.Pregnancy()` | Agents |

Networks and mixing pools can be used together, as a list, with a different β on each; `analyzers='infection_log'` records which route each infection came through (see [Analyzers](../user_guide/interventions_analyzers.qmd#the-infection-log)). [Mixing](../user_guide/populations_mixing.qmd) covers Starsim's other networks, including households (`ssl.ClusterNet`) and the [library's networks](../user_guide/library_networks.qmd). To make your own network, see [T8](t8_modules.qmd#a-network-written-as-code).

## Exercises

Exercises 1 and 2 use the town with age groups, and 3 to 5 networks.

1. Closing schools roughly halves the contacts between children. Change the matrix so that children have 5 contacts a day with other children instead of 10. How do the reproduction number at the start and the number infected in each age group change, and why?
2. Give every age group the same immunity, 90% (about the same overall share as above), keeping the contact matrix. How large is the outbreak now? What does this say about where gaps in immunity matter most?
3. Repeat the comparison of contacts per person with a rate of infection of 0.083 per contact per day (so R0 is about 2 with random mixing). How much does it matter now that people meet the same contacts every day, and why?
4. In the sexual network with partnerships that last a year, the infection dies out. Give the network `n_contacts=1` and `concurrency=0.2`, so that 20% of people have more than one partner at a time. Does the infection persist?
5. Add households of about 4 people (`ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(4))`, after `import starsim.library as ssl`) to measles with a community mixing pool of 2 contacts a day. How much of the epidemic do households add?

[Solutions](solutions.qmd#t4-mixing) · Next: [T5 – Interventions and scenarios](t5_interventions.qmd)

## Further reading

- [POLYMOD: Social contacts and mixing patterns relevant to the spread of infectious diseases](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0050074): the contact survey in eight European countries behind most age-structured models
- [socialmixr: Social mixing matrices for infectious disease modeling](https://epiforecasts.io/socialmixr/): an R package for building contact matrices from survey data
- [Xia, Bjørnstad and Grenfell (2004): Measles metapopulation dynamics: a gravity model for epidemiological coupling and dynamics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15278849/): the gravity model fitted to measles in England and Wales
- [EpiModel: network modeling for epidemics](https://epimodel.github.io/sismid/): a course on stochastic network models, including sexually transmitted infections, in R
